title: Esther 3:7–15
context: In the first month of the twelfth year of Ahasuerus, the lot (Pur) is cast before Haman day by day and month by month, and it falls on the twelfth month, Adar (3:7), leaving nearly a year before the planned day. Haman accuses an unnamed, scattered people of keeping different laws and not keeping the king’s, and offers ten thousand talents of silver, an enormous sum by any reckoning, for their destruction (3:8–9). The king gives Haman his signet ring and leaves the people and the silver in his hands (3:10–11); many readers take 3:11 as the king declining the silver, while others read it as the king granting Haman the use of the funds. On the thirteenth day of the first month the scribes write the decree in every script and language, sealed with the king’s ring, ordering the destruction, killing, and plunder of all Jews, young and old, on the thirteenth day of Adar (3:12–14). The king and Haman sit down to drink while the city of Susa is perplexed (3:15). Pur explains the later name of the feast of Purim (9:24–26). The book does not name God here, but readers in both traditions often see providence in the lot and in the long delay it produces; that is shared ground rather than a point of division. This commentary treats the decree soberly and names later reversals by reference (8:2, 8:9–14) without anticipating their details.

verses.text: In the first month, which is the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur, that is, the lot, before Haman from day to day, and from month to month, and chose the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman’s people cast Pur, the lot, to choose a day, and it falls on the twelfth month, almost a year away. Arminian readers note that the book never names God here and avoid treating the lot as a hidden message, yet many see God’s faithful care in the delay, which gives room for real human responses. Proverbs 16:33 is often cited as a canonical lens without being read into Haman’s intent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers frequently cite Proverbs 16:33 to affirm that even the lot falls under God’s governance, so that Haman’s divination unwittingly yields a delay that serves the preservation of the Jews. Shared ground: both traditions note that the book does not name God, that Pur later gives Purim its name (9:24–26), and that seeing providence in the lot is a common reading in both rather than a dividing line.

verses.text: Haman said to King Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom, and their laws are different from other people’s. They don’t keep the king’s laws. Therefore it is not for the king’s profit to allow them to remain.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman never names the people. He mixes truth (their laws differ) with falsehood (they do not keep the king’s laws) to make them sound dangerous. Arminian readers see the anatomy of slander, in which a half-truth is turned into a pretext, and they stress the moral responsibility both of the accuser and of a ruler who fails to ask questions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that faithfulness to God’s law can make a people look strange to the surrounding world (compare Daniel 6:5), and they read Haman’s charge as a distortion of that distinctiveness into disloyalty. Shared ground: both traditions highlight the deception in Haman’s speech, the danger of withholding the people’s name from the king, and the call to treat neighbors justly.

verses.text: If it pleases the king, let it be written that they be destroyed; and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who are in charge of the king’s business, to bring it into the king’s treasuries.”
verses.arminianNotes: Haman asks for a written decree of destruction and offers ten thousand talents of silver to the king’s treasuries. Arminian readers note that the size of the sum is clearly meant to be staggering, though its exact value is hard to fix, and they see the offer as an attempt to make a crime look profitable, which the king freely chooses not to examine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the vast offer as showing how deep Haman’s hatred runs, since he will pay a fortune to see a people destroyed. They note that greed and malice combine here, while God’s purposes for his people are not thwarted. Shared ground: both traditions avoid fixing the sum precisely, read it as an enormous amount, and note that 4:7 later recalls the exact figure.

verses.text: The king took his ring from his hand, and gave it to Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews’ enemy.
verses.arminianNotes: The king hands Haman his signet ring, the authority to issue decrees in his name, and the narrator calls Haman “the Jews’ enemy.” Arminian readers see a ruler abdicating moral responsibility by delegating life-and-death power without inquiry, and they note that the same ring will later pass to Mordecai (8:2), showing reversal through the unfolding of human decisions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the reversal at 8:2 and often read the passing of the ring as a sign that earthly authority, however absolute it seems, remains under God’s rule (compare Proverbs 21:1). Shared ground: both traditions take the narrator’s label “the Jews’ enemy” as defining Haman’s role in the story, and both notice the later return of the ring without needing God named here.

verses.text: The king said to Haman, “The silver is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king tells Haman that the silver is given to him and the people too, to do as he pleases. Readers differ on whether the king refuses the silver or lets Haman keep and use it; Esther’s later word “sold” (7:4) suggests to many readers that money remained part of the bargain. Arminian readers stress the king’s chilling indifference to the lives at stake, a real moral failure of his office.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the ambiguity about the silver and read the king’s words as handing over an entire people with a careless phrase. They see human authority here acting against its God-given purpose of restraining evil (compare Romans 13:3–4). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with sober grief at the casual way the decree is granted and leave the question of the silver open.

verses.text: Then the king’s scribes were called in on the first month, on the thirteenth day of the month; and all that Haman commanded was written to the king’s local governors, and to the governors who were over every province, and to the princes of every people, to every province according to its writing, and to every people in their language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus, and it was sealed with the king’s ring.
verses.arminianNotes: The scribes write the decree on the thirteenth day of the first month in every script and language, sealed with the king’s ring. Some readers note that this falls just before Passover on the fourteenth (Exodus 12:6). Arminian readers see the thoroughness of the bureaucracy as the scale of human evil once set in motion, and the date as a quiet reminder of past deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often draw out the same Passover echo, while noting that the narrator does not spell it out, and they read the machinery of empire as powerful yet still subject to God’s purposes. Shared ground: both traditions note that the decree is sealed with the king’s ring, which in Persian practice as the book presents it cannot be revoked (compare 8:8), and that the date echo is an inference.

verses.text: Letters were sent by couriers into all the king’s provinces, to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all Jews, both young and old, little children and women, in one day, even on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and to plunder their possessions.
verses.arminianNotes: The decree orders couriers to destroy, kill, and cause to perish all Jews, young and old, children and women, in one day, the thirteenth of Adar, and to take their goods. Arminian readers dwell soberly on the totality of the threat and on the moral evil of a state-sanctioned plan of destruction, which God neither wills nor approves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the decree as an assault on the covenant people and note that its threefold wording returns in the counter-decree of 8:11, a deliberate reversal. They hold that God permits such evil for a time while governing its outcome. Shared ground: both traditions name the decree as gravely evil, avoid sensationalizing it, and notice the verbal reversal later in the book.

verses.text: A copy of the letter, that the decree should be given out in every province, was published to all the peoples, that they should be ready against that day.
verses.arminianNotes: A copy of the decree is published to all the peoples so that they would be ready for that day. Arminian readers note that making the law public draws ordinary people across the empire into a moral choice, and that each person who prepares to obey it bears real responsibility. Public law can shape a culture toward violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the same public scope and note that the long interval before the appointed day leaves room for God’s preserving work, which the story will unfold. They see the publication as part of the scene in which deliverance will appear. Shared ground: both traditions read the publicity of the decree as raising the stakes for every province and preparing for the later counter-decree (8:13).

verses.text: The couriers went out in haste by the king’s commandment, and the decree was given out in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city of Susa was perplexed.
verses.arminianNotes: The couriers rush out, the king and Haman sit down to drink, and the city of Susa is perplexed. Arminian readers note the sharp contrast between the rulers’ ease and the citizens’ confusion, and they see the city’s unease as a sign that conscience still stirs among ordinary people, even under an unjust decree.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the contrast and read the scene as a portrait of the wicked at ease while judgment is prepared (compare Psalm 73:3–12), though the story will turn. Shared ground: both traditions read the perplexity of Susa as the narrator’s quiet moral verdict on the decree, and both note that the later joy of Susa in 8:15 answers this moment.
